newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Shipwreck that changed history excavated in Texas.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Shipwreck that changed history excavated in Texas.

text.p: Just off the Texas coast, archaeologists are painstakingly raising the remains of a wooden ship whose sinking more than three centuries ago may have changed the course of history.

The first layers of silt have been peeled off La Belle, which went down in Matagorda Bay during a winter storm in 1686, taking with it the last hopes of explorer Rene Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle, to colonise the area for France.

Researchers believe the wreck, found a year ago in 14 feet (4 metres) of water near Palacios about 90 miles (145 km) southwest of Houston, could yield valuable insight into La Salle's ill-fated expedition. They began excavation in September after a dam was built around the two-masted ship and bay waters were pumped out.

Inside the hull, workers have found muskets, lead shot, trinkets and the skeleton of a crewman who apparently died in the forward hold. The findings, along with extensive records of the ship's construction recently uncovered in France, are helping historians write the last chapter about a voyage they say could have turned the tide of history in the New World.

"This is one of those small events in history -- the sinking of a ship -- that caused a whole shift in U.S. history," Jim Bruseth, project director for the Texas Historical Commission, said. "If this expedition had been successful, we probably would be speaking French right now."

La Salle explored the Great Lakes region in the 1670s and is credited with discovering the mouth of the Mississippi River, in the process laying claim to half of the continent for France. Hoping to chart the mouth of the great river from the sea, he returned home in 1682 to mount a new expedition.

With four ships commissioned from King Louis XIV, La Salle set sail for what is now Louisiana in August 1684. But along the way, one ship was lost to pirates, another broke apart on a sand bar and a third returned home.

In January 1685, La Salle anchored his remaining ship, La Belle, in Matagorda Bay, thinking it was the mouth of the Mississippi, and took a crew ashore to establish a settlement. He soon realised he had missed his target and began leading land parties around the region searching for the lost river.

In January 1686, while its captain was drunk and La Salle off looking for the Mississippi, La Belle got caught in a winter storm and ran aground on a peninsula in the bay. The loss of the ship was the final straw for a crew that had endured hunger, disease and Indian attacks for more than a year. When La Salle set off for a French outpost in Illinois in search of help, his mutinous men killed him.

Although he failed to establish a permanent settlement, La Salle's expedition turned the tide of history. Spain launched a series of expeditions to cut short France's attempt to colonise what is now east Texas, accelerating settlement of the region. In the process, Spanish explorers found the wreckage of La Belle, looting the deck of five ornate bronze cannons and burning off her masts.

But rather than breaking apart to be lost forever, La Belle settled deep into the mud, preserving the contents of the lower third of her hull for archaeologists to find more than 300 years later. "This is one of the most exciting archaeological projects going on anywhere in the world," Bruseth said. "We're hoping to find an object that could be linked to La Salle directly."

So far, the archaeologists have uncovered the outline of the hull, exposing beams and the tops of barrels, crates and boxes in the cargo holds. In late October, they unearthed the nearly intact skeleton of a crewman lying in a large coil of anchor rope, an unopened cask by his side.

"It's entirely possible there are other people in there," said archaeologist John de Bry, founder of the Centre for Historical Archaeology in Melbourne Beach, Florida. Digging through archives in France, de Bry recently discovered the original construction papers for La Belle, a narrow-beam, shallow-draft boat that was a precursor of modern schooners.
"This is one of the most amazing projects I have ever worked on because there is so much historical data," he said.

The archaeologists now are in a race against time and money. About $4 million has been budgeted for the project, $3.1 million of it raised from donations and a state grant. But the costly excavation and work to preserve the remains once they are unearthed is quickly exhausting the funding.
"It's just too historically significant to shut things down before we excavate the hull," Bruseth said. "Whatever we don't get will probably be lost again to the sea."
